verdict.rationale: Three Greek word-stems (lemmas, the dictionary-form words) carry the proposition. The word 'head or source' (kephale, Strong's G2776) is predicated of the husband in Ephesians 5:23 and 1 Corinthians 11:3. The word 'be subject' (hypotasso, Strong's G5293), used here in middle voice (the form where the subject acts on or for themselves), is predicated of the wife in Ephesians 5:22 and 5:24, Colossians 3:18, 1 Peter 3:1 and 3:5, and Titus 2:5. The word 'love' (agapao, Strong's G0025), used as a present imperative (an ongoing command), is commanded of the husband in Ephesians 5:25, 5:28, and 5:33. The lemmas pattern with an asymmetric marriage ordering, but the precise force of the head metaphor is materially contested at the lexical level. 'Head or source' (kephale) denotes the anatomical head and is extended metaphorically in Pauline epistles. The classical Greek lexicon LSJ (Liddell-Scott-Jones) records the noun's literal sense set and gives the metaphorical extension to corporate heads through later usage, while the Hebrew 'head or chief or beginning' (rosh, Strong's H7218) that the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) routinely translates with 'head or source' (kephale) carries both a chief or leader sense and a beginning or front sense. The Pauline extension therefore inherits two defensible Koine (common-era Greek) readings, 'authority over' and 'source or origin', that the immediate context does not decisively rank. 'Be subject' (hypotasso) in the relevant texts is middle voice (the form where the subject acts on or for themselves), which places the act of ordering with the subject rather than imposing it externally, and Ephesians 5:21 'submitting to one another in the fear of Christ' (hypotassomenoi allelois en phobo Christou) immediately precedes and grammatically governs the wife clause in verse 22 which has no finite verb of its own. The husband side is not a right to command but 'love just as also Christ loved the church' (agapate kathos kai ho Christos egapesen ten ekklesian), with the husband told to love his wife as his own body. 1 Peter 3:7 names husband and wife 'joint-heirs of the grace of life' (sygkleronomoi charitos zoes). Because the headship lemma is two-valued and the surrounding household-code grammar frames the relation as reciprocal and love-bounded, the lexical data supports an asymmetric ordering in marriage but does not by itself settle the specific authority claim the stem assumes, so the verdict is disputed rather than a clean affirm or deny.

scripture.reasoning: 'Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ' (hypotassomenoi allelois en phobo Christou) is a present middle participle (an ongoing -ing form where the subject acts on or for themselves) whose plural subject is the same congregation addressed in Ephesians 5:18 to 5:20. Greek manuscript witnesses divide on whether verse 22 even contains a separate finite verb for wives, so verse 22 in the strongest witnesses grammatically borrows 'submitting' (hypotassomenoi) from verse 21. This governing participle places the wife clause inside a frame of mutual subjection and is the lexical hinge for any reading that resists fixed unilateral hierarchy in the household code that follows.

'The wives to their own husbands as to the Lord' (Hai gynaikes tois idiois andrasin hos to kyrio). The Greek of the strongest witnesses has no finite verb here, borrowing 'submitting' (hypotassomenoi) from verse 21, so the wife clause is grammatically chained to the mutual-submission frame. The qualifier 'own' (idiois) restricts the scope to the specific marriage bond rather than woman-to-man in general.

'Because the husband is head or source of the wife as also Christ is head or source of the assembly or church, he himself is savior of the body' (hoti aner estin kephale tes gynaikos hos kai ho Christos kephale tes ekklesias, autos soter tou somatos). The predicate 'head or source' (kephale) is asserted of the husband over the wife and paralleled to Christ as 'head or source' (kephale) of the assembly or church (ekklesia), then immediately qualified by 'he himself is savior of the body' (autos soter tou somatos). The savior tag attaches a protective and self-giving nuance to the head image rather than a bare assertion of rank. The lexical force of 'head or source' (kephale) here is the crux: Koine (common-era Greek) usage attests both an authority-over sense and a source or origin sense, and this verse alone does not disambiguate.

'But as the assembly or church is subject to Christ, so also the wives to the husbands in everything' (alla hos he ekklesia hypotassetai to Christo, houtos kai hai gynaikes tois andrasin en panti). 'Is subject' (hypotassetai) is middle-passive present indicative (an ongoing, simple statement of fact in the form where the subject acts on or for themselves or is acted upon), and the comparative 'as the assembly or church is subject' (hos he ekklesia hypotassetai) grounds the wife pattern in the church-to-Christ analogy. The middle voice (the form where the subject acts on or for themselves) carries voluntary self-ordering, not enforced subjugation, and the 'in everything' (en panti) clause sets the scope without supplying a sense of compulsion.

'Husbands, love the wives, just as also Christ loved the assembly or church and gave himself up for her' (Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas, kathos kai ho Christos egapesen ten ekklesian kai heauton paredoken hyper autes). 'Love' (agapate) is present active imperative (an ongoing command in the active form) directed at husbands, qualified by the 'just as' (kathos) clause that grounds the love in Christ's self-giving for the assembly or church. The husband duty is sacrificial love measured by Christ, which converts any head function into a self-spending vocation rather than a prerogative.

'So also husbands ought to love their own wives as their own bodies' (houtos opheilousin kai hoi andres agapan tas heauton gynaikas hos ta heauton somata). The body identification dissolves a strict over-under hierarchy into a one-flesh care obligation: 'the one loving his own wife loves himself' (ho agapon ten heautou gynaika heauton agapa). Loving the wife is loving the husband's own body, which collapses competitive interests inside the head-body figure.

'For this reason a man shall leave the father and the mother and shall be joined to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh' (anti toutou kataleipsei anthropos ton patera kai ten metera kai proskollethesetai pros ten gynaika autou, kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian), citing Genesis 2:24. The one-flesh formula is brought into the head-body argument so that the head and the body share one 'flesh' (sarx), foreclosing any reading of headship as ontological separation (separation in essential being) between a higher partner and a lower partner.

'Nevertheless, you also, each one, let him love his own wife as himself, and let the wife respect the husband' (plen kai hymeis hoi kath' hena hekastos ten heautou gynaika houtos agapato hos heauton, he de gyne hina phobetai ton andra). The summary pairs husband 'let him love' (agapato) with wife 'let her respect or reverently regard' (phobetai), an asymmetric pairing of love-command and respect-response within the marriage relation rather than a command-and-obey pairing.

'But I want you to know that of every man the head or source is Christ, and head or source of woman is the man, and head or source of Christ is God' (thelo de hymas eidenai hoti pantos andros he kephale ho Christos estin, kephale de gynaikos ho aner, kephale de tou Christou ho theos). The chain Christ-of-man, man-of-woman, God-of-Christ uses 'head or source' (kephale) uniformly across all three relations. Because the same lemma governs the God-Christ relation, the sense cannot be reduced to simple boss-over-subordinate without straining Christology (the doctrine of who Christ is). Whatever sense the second pair carries must also fit the third, which is exactly why 'head or source' (kephale) is lexically disputed: an authority-over reading must be qualified so that it does not subordinate the Son in essential being (ontologically), and a source-of reading must be qualified so that it still carries directional ordering.

'Wives, be subject to the husbands as is fitting in the Lord' (Hai gynaikes, hypotassesthe tois andrasin hos aneken en kyrio). 'Be subject' (hypotassesthe) is present middle imperative (an ongoing command in the form where the subject acts on or for themselves); the qualifier 'as is fitting' (hos aneken) bounds the obedience to what is appropriate in the Lord, not absolute. The very next verse pairs it with husbands' obligation to love and not be embittered, so the lexical pattern is asymmetric directives, not asymmetric essential being (ontology).

'Husbands, love the wives and do not be embittered against them' (Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas kai me pikrainesthe pros autas). The husband imperative is paired with a prohibition on bitterness, restraining any exercise of headship that would harm the wife. The lemma 'love' (agapate) echoes the Ephesians 5:25 frame and confirms that the husband side of the household code is love and gentleness, not command rights.

'Likewise wives, submitting to your own husbands' (Homoios gynaikes, hypotassomenai tois idiois andrasin). The middle participle (the -ing form where the subject acts on or for themselves) matches Ephesians and Colossians, with 'own' (idiois) again restricting scope to the marriage bond. The continuation 'so that even if some are disobedient to the word, through the conduct of the wives they may be won without a word' (hina kai ei tines apeithousin to logo, dia tes ton gynaikon anastrophes aneu logou kerdethesontai) frames submission as missional persuasion of unbelieving husbands rather than enforced silence.

'Husbands, likewise dwelling together with knowledge, as with a weaker vessel, the female, assigning honor, as also being joint-heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered' (Hoi andres homoios synoikountes kata gnosin, hos asthenestero skeuei to gynaikeio aponemontes timen, hos kai sygkleronomois charitos zoes, eis to me egkoptesthai tas proseuchas hymon). Husbands are commanded to dwell with knowledge, assign honor to the wife as a 'weaker vessel' (asthenestero skeuei), and treat her as 'joint-heir' (sygkleronomos) of the grace of life. The lemma 'joint-heir' (sygkleronomos) asserts equal share in salvation, which complicates any reading of headship as ontological superiority (superiority in essential being) while leaving the asymmetric directive structure intact.

'For Adam was formed first, then Eve' (Adam gar protos eplasthe, eita Heua). The temporal 'first' (protos) and 'then' (eita) pair invokes the Genesis 2 creation order to ground the prior instruction. Lexically, the argument hangs on chronology of forming, not on essential rank, and the same lemma cluster appears in 1 Corinthians 11:8-9 with the qualification in 1 Corinthians 11:11-12 that 'neither is woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord' (ouk estin gyne choris andros oude aner choris gynaikos en kyrio), neither is independent of the other in the Lord. So the creation-order appeal carries asymmetric ordering but is explicitly bounded by mutual dependence in the same lemma field.

complicating_texts.resolution: The participle 'submitting to one another in the fear of Christ' (hypotassomenoi allelois en phobo Christou) immediately precedes the household code and grammatically governs the wife clause in verse 22, which lacks a finite verb of its own in the strongest manuscript witnesses. The mutual-submission framing is the lexical ground for the egalitarian reading of the household code and means the wife submission is set inside a broader reciprocity. The complementarian reading takes 'to one another' (alleloi) here distributively rather than mutually, citing parallels where 'to one another' (alleloi) means some to others rather than each to each, but the simpler reading is mutual. This text constrains the verdict toward disputed.

The joint-heir designation 'joint-heirs of the grace of life' (sygkleronomois charitos zoes) places husband and wife as equal recipients of grace, so any headship in the stem is bounded by spiritual co-equality and honor rather than rank superiority. The 'weaker vessel' (asthenestero skeuei) reference describes relative physical vulnerability and does not name a hierarchy in essential being (ontological hierarchy). This constrains but does not erase the ordered pattern of asymmetric directives, contributing to the disputed verdict.

The lexical sense of 'head or source' (kephale) in this verse remains underdetermined by morphology (word-form) and immediate syntax. The classical Greek lexicon LSJ (Liddell-Scott-Jones) for 'head or source' (kephale) records the literal anatomical sense richly attested from Homer onward and notes the Hebrew 'head or chief or beginning' (rosh) underlying Greek Old Testament usage. The Hebrew 'head or chief or beginning' (rosh, Strong's H7218) carries both a chief or leader sense and a beginning or front sense, and the Pauline metaphorical extension legitimately inherits either. The same Greek lemma governs the God-Christ pair in the same series, which means whichever sense is chosen must avoid subordinating the Son in essential being (ontological subordination). The verse therefore attests a 'head or source' (kephale) relation in marriage but does not by itself rank between authority and source, leaving the headship sense lexically disputed.

'However, neither is woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord' (plen oute gyne choris andros oute aner choris gynaikos en kyrio). The 'however, neither' (plen oute) construction explicitly limits any one-directional reading of verse 3 with a strong mutual-dependence claim within the same lemma field ('husband or man' (aner), 'wife or woman' (gyne)). This is the immediate context that disciplines an unbounded authority-over reading of the 'head or source' (kephale) chain in verse 3.

variant_units_examined.note: The strongest witnesses omit a separate finite 'be subject' (hypotassesthe) in verse 22 and require it to be borrowed from the verse 21 participle. Later witnesses supply the verb. Either way the wife clause depends grammatically on verse 21, so the verdict on the proposition is not flipped, but the grammatical link to verse 21 mutual submission is strengthened in the shorter reading.

variants.note: These passages fall outside the ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) 3 John CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) sample, so collation is at shadow level. The apparatus marks in Ephesians 5:22 to 5:33 and 1 Peter 3 mostly concern word order and minor additions and do not flip the head, submit, or love lemmas that carry the verdict. The verse 22 verb variant nudges the grammar toward the mutual-submission framing of verse 21.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'head or source' (kephale, Strong's G2776) in Ephesians 5:23 and 1 Corinthians 11:3 in its attested authority-over sense, drawing on Pauline parallels where Christ as 'head or source' (kephale) of the assembly or church and head over all things (Ephesians 1:22, Colossians 1:18, Colossians 2:10) carries a clear governance sense. Reads 'be subject' (hypotasso, Strong's G5293) as ordered response to that headship, parallel to the assembly or church to Christ in Ephesians 5:24, with the middle voice (the form where the subject acts on or for themselves) marking willing but real subordination rather than coerced silence. Reads the creation-order argument in 1 Timothy 2:13 ('Adam was formed first, then Eve' / Adam protos eplasthe, eita Heua) as Pauline grounding for the household pattern in the original Genesis order, and the household codes in Colossians 3:18-19, Titus 2:5, and 1 Peter 3:1-6 as a consistent canonical pattern. On this reading the lemmas land directly on the stem: loving headship in the husband and willing submission in the wife, both inside the Christ-church analogy.

Reads 'head or source' (kephale, Strong's G2776) in its attested source or origin sense, drawing on the Hebrew 'head or chief or beginning' (rosh, Strong's H7218) sense set that includes beginning and front, and arguing that the Christ-assembly or church figure in Ephesians 5:23 emphasizes Christ as source of the assembly or church's life rather than ruler over it, given the immediate qualifier 'he himself is savior of the body' (autos soter tou somatos). Foregrounds the present middle participle (an ongoing -ing form where the subject acts on or for themselves) 'submitting to one another' (hypotassomenoi allelois) in Ephesians 5:21 as the governing verb of verse 22 and reads 'to one another' (alleloi) mutually, placing the entire household code inside reciprocal subjection. Reads the love-command of Ephesians 5:25-29 and the joint-heir designation 'joint-heir' (sygkleronomos) in 1 Peter 3:7 as flattening any fixed hierarchy. Treats the household codes as Spirit-shaped accommodation to a hierarchical first-century setting and reads Galatians 3:28 ('there is neither male and female, for you all are one in Christ Jesus' / ouk eni arsen kai thely, panta gar hymeis heis este en Christo Iesou) as the eschatological (end-time) horizon that relativizes role-based authority. On this reading the lemmas attest an asymmetric pattern but do not carry the specific authority claim the stem assumes.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on a single lexeme (dictionary-form word) 'head or source' (kephale, Strong's G2776), whose Koine (common-era Greek) metaphorical extension is two-valued ('authority over' and 'source or origin'), and on the grammatical scope of the governing participle 'submitting' (hypotassomenoi) in Ephesians 5:21. Both lenses share the same morphology (word-form analysis) of the passages and read the same lemmas. They differ on which attested sense of 'head or source' (kephale) Paul activates, and on how broadly the 'to one another' (alleloi) of verse 21 governs the household code. The principle of comparing Scripture with Scripture (analogia_scripturae) is the decisive move on both sides: complementarian reads from 1 Timothy 2:13 and Ephesians 1:22 inward; egalitarian reads from Ephesians 5:21 and Galatians 3:28 inward. The lemmas alone do not rank these moves.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Within marriage, the husband is called 'head or source' (kephale) of the wife and the wife is called to 'be subject' (hypotasso) to him, while the husband is commanded to 'love' (agapao) the wife. The precise force of 'head or source' (kephale), whether authority over or source or origin, and the scope of the wife response are what the lexical data must decide on the original stem.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem loads the verdict with the phrases 'loving headship' and 'willing submission', both 'in mutual love and Christ-likeness', which already presupposes a specific complementarian sense of 'head or source' (kephale) and a particular voluntariness reading of 'be subject' (hypotasso). The neutralized form names the three Greek lexemes (dictionary-form words) without resolving the contested 'head or source' (kephale) sense, so the verdict is derived on the words rather than on the framing. The verdict is assessed against the original stem and lands disputed because 'head or source' (kephale) carries two attested Koine (common-era Greek) senses and the surrounding 'to one another' (alleloi) grammar plus the husband's love duty plus the 'joint-heir' (sygkleronomos) status do not ratify the authority sense over the source sense at the word level. lay_summary: Three Greek words carry this question. The husband is called the head, 'head or source' (kephale), in Ephesians 5:23 and 1 Corinthians 11:3. The wife is told to be subject, 'be subject' (hypotasso), in Ephesians 5:22 and 5:24, Colossians 3:18, and 1 Peter 3:1 and 3:5. The husband is commanded to love, 'love' (agapao), in Ephesians 5:25, 5:28, and 5:33 and Colossians 3:19. The wording lines up with an ordered marriage, but the meaning of head is the sticking point. In Koine (common-era) Greek 'head or source' (kephale) can mean the one in authority over a group, and it can also mean the source or origin, like the head of a river. The Hebrew word it usually translates in the Old Testament, 'head or chief or beginning' (rosh), carries both senses too. The verses themselves do not settle which sense Paul activates, and in 1 Corinthians 11:3 the same word also describes how God relates to Christ, which makes a bare boss-over-worker reading awkward without further qualification. Several features push against reading head as plain rank. The submission verb is in the middle voice (the form where the subject acts on or for themselves), which points to a freely chosen self-ordering rather than coercion. The sentence just before the household code, Ephesians 5:21, tells everyone to submit to one another, and that participle grammatically controls the wife clause in verse 22 in the strongest manuscript witnesses. The husband side is not a right to command but a duty to love his wife the way Christ gave himself up for the assembly or church (ekklesia), and to love her as his own body, with Colossians 3:19 adding the prohibition on being embittered against her. In 1 Peter 3:7 the wife is called a joint-heir, 'joint-heir' (sygkleronomos), of the grace of life and the husband is told to assign her honor, so the two stand equal before God even within an ordered relationship. The lexical root of the dispute is therefore simple: a key word has two well-attested senses, and the surrounding text disciplines both senses without picking one. The pattern in the words clearly supports an asymmetric, love-shaped marriage order, but does not by itself prove the specific authority claim the proposition assumes, so the verdict is genuinely contested at the word level rather than cleanly settled in either direction.
